column1: # Hidden souvenirs. One per line, tab separated: id, region, kind (A attraction, D dish, C culture), the English name of the stop that hides it, Chinese name, English name, story, and optionally pinyin (otherwise made automatically).
# A souvenir is found when its stop is unlocked. DRAFT: written from general knowledge, not fact-checked. Pictures: tools/souvenir-art.js

column7: A soft black-and-white keepsake from the base where giant pandas are raised. Wild pandas live only in the mountains of Sichuan, Shaanxi and Gansu.
A saucer, a bowl and a lid. You tilt the lid to hold back the leaves and sip through the gap.
In Sichuan opera an actor swaps painted faces in a blink. How it is done has long been a closely guarded secret of the troupes.
A slab of chilies, Sichuan pepper and beef fat that melts into the broth. Take it home and you can make a little Chongqing in your own pot.
A copy of one of the bronze masks with wide, jutting eyes found at Sanxingdui, a city of the ancient Shu people more than 3,000 years old.
The colours tell you about the character: red often shows loyalty and courage, white a crafty, scheming one.

column6: Tu'er Ye, the clay rabbit lord
column7: A clay rabbit in armor, an old Beijing toy for the Mid-Autumn Festival. Folk tales say a rabbit once cured a plague in the city.
Thin copper wires are bent into patterns, filled with colored enamel and fired. The name means "Jingtai blue", after the Jingtai reign of the Ming dynasty.
A chubby baby holding a carp is a wish for a year of plenty. Yangliuqing, near Tianjin, has printed and hand-painted these for centuries.
A tiny painted clay person with a lively face. The Zhang family workshop in Tianjin began in the 1800s.
Purple clay from Yixing, near Wuxi, is left unglazed. Tea lovers say a pot slowly takes on the flavor of the tea it brews.
A fat, smiling boy from the Huishan clay toys of Wuxi, kept as a lucky charm to protect children.
Silk threads split into fine strands make a kitten's fur look soft. The best Suzhou pieces are stitched so that both sides show the picture.
A brocade woven with gold thread, once made for the imperial court. The name means "cloud brocade" because it shimmers like sunset clouds.
A little silk qipao on a hanger. The slim, high-collared dress became fashionable in Shanghai in the 1920s and 1930s.
A plate painted in bright enamel and gold. Guangcai ware was made in Guangzhou, much of it for sale overseas.
A red paper cut of a dancing lion. Foshan paper cuts are known for bold colors and a sparkle of metal foil.
A dark, smooth stone from Zhaoqing for grinding ink. Calligraphers have prized it since the Tang dynasty.
A training post with three wooden arms and one leg, used to practice Wing Chun's close-range moves.
The classic present to bring home from Taiwan: a buttery pastry with a sweet pineapple filling. In Taiwanese the fruit's name is said to sound like "prosperity comes".
A hand puppet with a carved wooden head and embroidered robes. The name, budaixi, means "cloth-bag theater".
Wishes are written on the paper before the lantern floats up. Pingxi, near Shifen, is the place for it.
Tea grown high on Alishan, among cool mist. A tin like this keeps the leaves fresh.
In the Legend of the White Snake, set at West Lake, an umbrella in the rain brings the scholar Xu Xian and the white snake spirit together.
A cup with a soft green glaze that people compare to jade. Longquan has made celadon for around a thousand years or more.
The Hu brush is the "brush" in the Four Treasures of the Study: Hu brush, Hui ink, Xuan paper and Duan inkstone.
Cloth is tied in knots, dipped in blue plant dye and opened to show white flower patterns. A craft of the Bai people of Dali.
Tea leaves pressed into a round cake wrapped in paper. Pu'er is a tea that people age on purpose, like wine.
Dongba is a picture writing of the Naxi people: little drawings of birds, people and flowers stand for words.
A hand-held wheel that people spin clockwise as they walk the Barkhor circuit around the Jokhang Temple.
A silk scarf offered to guests and teachers as a sign of respect and good wishes.
A wooden bowl for mixing tsampa, roasted barley flour, with butter tea, kneaded by hand into a dough.
Threads are tie-dyed before weaving, which gives this Uyghur silk its feathery, blurred patterns.
A small embroidered cap worn by Uyghur men and women. Shapes and patterns differ from place to place.
A long-necked lute with a round body, played in Uyghur music, including the Twelve Muqam.
A pocket-size soldier. The real army was buried near Emperor Qin Shi Huang's tomb about 2,200 years ago, and it is said that no two faces match.
A figure cut from thin, see-through leather and moved on sticks behind a lit screen. Shaanxi is one of the homes of shadow plays.
A little model of the pagoda built in the Tang dynasty to keep the Buddhist scriptures that the monk Xuanzang brought from India.
A sturdy woven bag with red, white and blue stripes. Hong Kong people use it for everything, from shopping to moving house.
Hong Kong's double-decker trams have run since 1904 and are nicknamed for the sound of their bell.
A small cage of bamboo or wood. Keeping songbirds is an old pastime, and this garden market is full of them.
A round earthen building where a whole Hakka clan lived, with rooms around a shared courtyard like a small village.
A soft, colorful stone from Shoushan near Fuzhou, much loved for carving into personal seals.
A tiny pot and small cups for brewing tea again and again. Gongfu tea is a custom of southern Fujian and Chaoshan.
Before paper, books were strips of bamboo tied with cord. Early copies of the Analects, which record Confucius' sayings, would have looked like this.
Weifang calls itself the kite capital of the world and holds an international kite festival.
The stone front is all that is left of a church that burned down in 1835.
Crumbly almond biscuits packed in a tin are a favorite gift from Macau.
The Vanda Miss Joaquim orchid is Singapore's national flower, named after Agnes Joaquim, who grew it in her garden in the 1890s.
Peranakan women stitched tiny glass beads into flowers and butterflies on their slippers. The craft is called kasut manek.
Sancai means "three colors": green, amber and cream glazes. Luoyang is famous for these Tang dynasty pottery horses and camels.
The oldest known Chinese writing was carved on turtle shells and animal bones more than 3,000 years ago, and much of it was found at Anyang.
Hunan cooks love chili in nearly every dish, and strings of red chilies hang drying outside village houses.
Yuelu Academy is about a thousand years old, one of the great old schools of Chinese learning. A famous couplet hangs at its gate.
Miao silverwork is worn on festival days, from bracelets to towering headdresses. The more silver, the finer the festival outfit.
A mouth organ of bamboo pipes, played and danced to at Miao and Dong festivals.
A silk ball with tassels that young Zhuang people toss to each other at song festivals. It is also a symbol of love.
Packets of river-snail rice noodles from Liuzhou travel all over China. Opening one fills the room with a sour smell that people either love or flee.
A thin cup cut from green stone, said to glow in the moonlight. A Tang dynasty poem about drinking wine on the frontier mentions one.
A heavenly musician painted flying with streaming ribbons, as seen in the cave paintings at Dunhuang.
Cobalt blue painted on white clay, fired at high heat. Jingdezhen was the great center for making it.
In autumn, Wuyuan villagers dry peppers, pumpkins and corn on round bamboo trays set on roofs and walls. The colorful sight is called shaiqiu.
Bronze bells hung in rows, like the set from the tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng. They can still play tunes after more than 2,400 years.
A two-stringed fiddle with a carved horse head at the top, played on the grassland.
A round felt tent made to be taken down and carried to fresh pasture.
Shanxi vinegar is aged for years in jars, which gives it a dark color and a rich sour taste. Shanxi people are said to love it.
A black lacquer box polished by hand until it shines like a mirror. Pushed-light lacquerware is a craft of Pingyao.
A green-yellow jade from Xiuyan county, carved into pendants and little Buddhas.
Errenzhuan performers twirl a bright handkerchief in time with the music. It is loud, funny northeastern folk theater for two.
A lantern made of ice with a light inside is a Harbin winter tradition, said to have begun as a custom of local farmers and fishers.
Painted wooden dolls that open to show smaller ones. Harbin has strong Russian links, and its shops sell them.
Craftspeople carve coconut shells into bowls, vases and lanterns. It is a traditional craft of Hainan.
Cloth woven by Li women from threads dyed in bright colors. UNESCO has recognized Li textile skills as intangible heritage.
Ink sticks of soot and glue were a specialty of Huizhou. A good one is said to stay black for centuries.
Pictures made by forging iron, hammered and welded into pines, plum branches and mountains. A craft of Wuhu.
Changbai Mountain is famous for ginseng, a root long used in Chinese medicine. The name 人参 means "person root", for its shape.
Ningxia is famous for goji berries, small red fruits added to soups and teas.
At Chaka Salt Lake a thin sheet of water over white salt mirrors the sky. A crystal of salt is its keepsake.
